`chunks(v, n)` should split a vector into consecutive pieces of at most `n` elements (the last may be shorter) and return them as views. Throw an `ArgumentError` if `n` is not positive. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
function chunks(v::AbstractVector, n::Integer)
    n > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("chunk size must be positive, got $n"))
    return [view(v, i:min(i + n - 1, lastindex(v))) for i in firstindex(v):n:lastindex(v)]
end
```

Remove consecutive duplicates from a vector, keeping the first of each run: `[1,1,2,2,2,3,1]` becomes `[1,2,3,1]`. Name it `dedupe_runs`. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
function dedupe_runs(v::AbstractVector)
    out = similar(v, 0)
    for x in v
        (isempty(out) || !isequal(last(out), x)) && push!(out, x)
    end
    return out
end
```

Write `histcounts(xs, edges)`: for sorted bin edges, count how many values of `xs` fall in each half-open bin `[edges[i], edges[i+1])`. Values outside all bins are ignored. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
function histcounts(xs, edges::AbstractVector)
    length(edges) >= 2 || throw(ArgumentError("need at least two edges"))
    issorted(edges) || throw(ArgumentError("edges must be sorted"))
    counts = zeros(Int, length(edges) - 1)
    for x in xs
        i = searchsortedlast(edges, x)
        1 <= i < length(edges) && (counts[i] += 1)
    end
    return counts
end
```

Implement a minimal parametric `Stack{T}` with `push!`, `pop!`, `isempty` and `length`. Popping an empty stack throws an `ArgumentError`. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
struct Stack{T}
    items::Vector{T}
end
Stack{T}() where {T} = Stack{T}(T[])

Base.push!(s::Stack, x) = (push!(s.items, x); s)
Base.pop!(s::Stack) = isempty(s.items) ? throw(ArgumentError("stack is empty")) : pop!(s.items)
Base.isempty(s::Stack) = isempty(s.items)
Base.length(s::Stack) = length(s.items)
```

Write `format_bytes(n)` that turns a non-negative byte count into text with binary units, e.g. `format_bytes(1536)` gives `"1.5 KiB"` and `format_bytes(12)` gives `"12 B"`. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
function format_bytes(n::Integer)
    n >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("byte count must be non-negative, got $n"))
    units = ("B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB", "PiB")
    x = float(n)
    i = 1
    while x >= 1024 && i < length(units)
        x /= 1024
        i += 1
    end
    return i == 1 ? string(n, " B") : string(round(x; digits = 1), " ", units[i])
end
```

Write a function `mode_of(v)` returning the most frequent element, the smallest one if there is a tie, and throwing an `ArgumentError` on empty input. Only the function, no tests.

```julia
function mode_of(v)
    isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("empty collection"))
    counts = Dict{eltype(v),Int}()
    for x in v
        counts[x] = get(counts, x, 0) + 1
    end
    best = maximum(values(counts))
    return minimum(k for (k, c) in counts if c == best)
end
```

Write `trim_trailing_zeros(v)` returning `v` without its trailing zero entries (an empty vector if all are zero). Give me only the function: no tests, no usage examples, no explanation.

```julia
function trim_trailing_zeros(v::AbstractVector)
    last_nonzero = findlast(!iszero, v)
    return isnothing(last_nonzero) ? v[1:0] : v[firstindex(v):last_nonzero]
end
```

Write `pnorm(v, p = 2)`, the p-norm of a vector, where `p = Inf` gives the maximum absolute value and `p < 1` is rejected with an `ArgumentError`. No tests please, only the function.

```julia
function pnorm(v, p::Real = 2)
    p >= 1 || throw(ArgumentError("p must be at least 1, got $p"))
    isinf(p) && return maximum(abs, v)
    return sum(x -> abs(x)^p, v)^(1 / p)
end
```

In one sentence: what does the `!` at the end of a name like `sort!` mean?
By convention it marks a function that may modify one or more of its arguments, so `sort!(v)` sorts `v` in place while `sort(v)` returns a new sorted array.
Answer in one sentence: what is the difference between `==` and `===`?

`==` tests equality as each type defines it (so `1 == 1.0` is `true`), while `===` tests whether two values are indistinguishable, which for mutable objects means they are the same object (so `1 === 1.0` is `false`).
One sentence only: why is the first call of a Julia function slower than the later calls?
The first call with a given combination of argument types has to compile a specialized method, and later calls with the same types reuse that compiled code.
In a single sentence, what does `eachindex(A)` return for a plain `Matrix`?

For a plain `Matrix` it returns `Base.OneTo(length(A))`, a range of linear indices, whereas for arrays without fast linear indexing, such as a two-dimensional view or an adjoint, it returns `CartesianIndices`.
One sentence: when should a global variable be declared `const`?
Declare a global `const` when its value (or at least its type) will not change, because functions that read it can then be compiled with a known type instead of treating it as `Any`.
Explain in one sentence what a `Union{Nothing, T}` return type is for.
It describes a result that is either a value of type `T` or `nothing` to signal that there is no value, as `findfirst` does when nothing matches.
